cues.text: Welcome back.
In this class we will work through mass weighted positions, axis theorems,
angular momentum, beam equilibrium and rolling down an incline.
Imagine two small masses joined by a light connector.
Their centre of mass is a mass weighted position, not necessarily the
midpoint.
Put 2 kg at x equals 0 and 3 kg at x equals 4 m.
Multiply each position by its mass, add, then divide by total mass: (2 times 0
plus 3 times 4)/5 equals 2.4 m.
The answer lies nearer the heavier mass.
For positive masses on a line it must lie between the extreme positions; that
is a useful check before trusting your arithmetic.
Use the same weighted average separately for x, y and z components.
A uniform straight rod has its centre of mass at its midpoint, but a
nonuniform
rod may not.
For a continuous body, replace the particle sum by an integral over mass.
Symmetry is often quicker: a uniform ring has its centre of mass at its
geometric centre even though there is no material there.
For a fixed mass system, the net external force equals total mass times centre
of mass acceleration.
Internal forces can rearrange the particles but cannot by themselves change
the
total momentum.
On a horizontal frictionless surface, a person walking along a movable
platform
shifts the platform oppositely while their combined horizontal centre of mass
stays fixed if initially at rest.
Always include both person and platform in that system.
Moment of inertia sums mass times squared perpendicular distance from the
chosen axis.
For standard uniform bodies, identify the axis before choosing a formula.
A thin ring about its central perpendicular axis has I equals MR squared; a
uniform disk has I equals MR squared/2.
A uniform solid sphere about a diameter has 2MR squared/5, while a thin
spherical shell has 2MR squared/3.
A uniform thin rod has ML squared/12 about a perpendicular midpoint axis.
These shapes and axes are part of each formula.
The parallel axis theorem moves from an axis through the centre of mass to a
parallel axis a distance d away: I equals the centre of mass moment of inertia
plus Md squared.
For a 3 kg uniform rod of length 2 m, midpoint inertia is
1 kilogram metre squared.
Move to a perpendicular axis through its end: d equals 1 m, so the end axis
moment of inertia equals 1 plus 3 equals 4 kilogram metre squared.
Do not use the distance between arbitrary nonparallel axes.
Starting from two off centre axes also requires knowing their distances from
the centre of mass axis, not blindly adding Md squared between them.
For a thin planar lamina, the perpendicular axis theorem states I z equals I x
plus I y for two perpendicular in plane axes intersecting at the point where
the normal z axis passes.
It does not apply to an arbitrary three dimensional body.
A uniform disk has equal diameter axis inertias by symmetry, so each is
MR squared/4.
Radius of gyration is a length defined by I equals Mradius of gyration
squared.
It locates an equivalent inertia distance, not necessarily a physical ring of
material.
For a particle, angular momentum about a point is r cross p.
Its magnitude is mvr sin(theta), where theta is the angle between position and
velocity.
The perpendicular distance from the reference point to the particle's straight
line path is often easier: magnitude equals mv times that distance.
A 2 kg particle moving at 3 metres per second on a straight path 0.5 m from
the origin has angular momentum magnitude 3 kilogram metre squared per second,
even though it is not moving in a circle.
About a fixed point in an inertial frame, the net external torque equals the
rate of change of total angular momentum.
If that torque vanishes, angular momentum is conserved.
For rotation about a fixed principal or symmetry axis, the axial component is
I
omega.
Do not assume the vector angular momentum is parallel to angular velocity for
every possible axis of a three dimensional body.
An isolated rotating system reduces its axial moment of inertia from 4 to 2
kilogram metre squared, starting at 3 radians per second, with negligible
external torque about that axis.
Initial angular momentum is 12 kilogram metre squared per second.
The final angular speed is 6 radians per second.
Does its rotational kinetic energy stay unchanged?
Pause and compare.
It rises from 18 to 36 J.
Internal work during the rearrangement supplies the increase.
Conservation of angular momentum does not automatically conserve rotational
kinetic energy.
A rigid body in static equilibrium needs both zero net external force and zero
net external torque.
Balanced forces alone do not prevent turning.
Two equal opposite parallel forces on different lines of action form a couple:
net force is zero but their torques can add.
Choose a torque reference that removes an unknown reaction, then still check
the force equation.
Consider a horizontal uniform 4 m beam of mass 2 kg supported vertically at
both ends.
A 6 kg load sits 1 m from the left end.
Use g equals 10 metres per second squared and neglect support friction.
The beam weight is 20 N at its midpoint; the load weight is 60 N at x equals 1
m.
Call the upward reactions the left reaction and the right reaction.
Vertical equilibrium gives their sum as 80 N.
Take torques about the left support, positive anticlockwise.
The left reaction has zero lever arm.
The right reaction contributes 4the right reaction; the two downward weights
contribute minus 20 times 2 and minus 60 times 1.
Therefore 4the right reaction equals 100, giving the right reaction equals 25
N
and the left reaction equals 55 N.
The larger reaction is near the load.
If a support can only push, a calculated negative reaction would invalidate
the
assumed contact; do not quietly accept a downward normal force.
Release a uniform solid cylinder from rest down a fixed rough incline.
Assume pure rolling on a stationary surface, sufficient static friction, no
deformation losses and no rolling resistance.
The centre accelerates downhill while static friction points uphill and
supplies torque about the centre.
Translational force balance gives mg sin(theta) minus f equals ma.
Torque gives fR equals the centre of mass moment of inertia alpha, and no slip
gives a equals R alpha.
Combining them yields a equals g sin(theta)/(1 plus the centre of mass
moment of inertia divided by mass times radius squared).
For a solid cylinder the centre of mass moment of inertia is mass times radius
squared divided by two.
At 30 degrees with g equals 10 metres per second squared, its acceleration is
10/3 metres per second squared, not 5 metres per second squared.
Some gravitational energy goes into rotation, so the centre accelerates less
than a frictionless sliding particle.
In ideal pure rolling the instantaneous contact point is stationary relative
to
the fixed surface.
Static friction therefore does no net work on the rigid body here, although it
redistributes translational and rotational energy.
This conclusion need not hold for a moving surface.
The required friction is mg sin(theta)/3 for the cylinder, while N equals mg
cos(theta).
Hence the no slip condition is the coefficient of static friction must be at
least tan(theta)/3.
Below that coefficient, the rolling assumption fails and sliding must be
treated separately.
After a vertical drop h, energy gives v squared equals 2gh/(1
plus the centre of mass moment of inertia divided by mass times radius
squared).
A solid cylinder dropping 0.30 m with g equals 10 reaches 2 metres per second.
A ring has a different inertia and a different final speed.
Compare models, not just masses.
